Ultimately, whether traveling with a toddler is easier than with a baby depends on the individual child's temperament and the type of trip. Some parents find toddlers easier to manage during travel due to their increased independence. Travel with a toddler can be rewarding, offering opportunities for learning and bonding.

item.instruction: Is it easier to travel with a baby or a toddler?
item.reference: Most people have found that traveling is a baby is much easier. This is largely because they are not yet fully mobile and haven't learned to walk or run just yet. Babies are considered infants under the age of 1. Traveling with a baby or a toddler still requires a lot of "stuff", but babies are typically more easily entertained by everyday random objects, such as a cup, or a napkin, etc, whereas toddlers are further along in the developmental journey and need more stimulation, especially on a long journey. Babies are also small enough to wear in a baby carrier, leaving parents hands-free to be able to juggle the copious amounts of luggage and toys needed when traveling with little ones. Babies are typically easier to travel with on planes as they still sleep for more hours than they're typically awake. According to many studies, the ideal age to travel with children is between 4 months to a year.

item.instruction: What Peloton instructor should I take a cycling class with for the following moods and why? Happy, Sad, Angry, Unmotivated
item.reference: There are 48 Peloton instructors who teach a variety of classes including: strength, tread, cycling, yoga, boxing, rowing, running, stretching, meditation, cardio, pilates, barre, and bootcamp. They have both male and female instructors representing a variety of body types. The classes are high energy in nature and feature music from todays hits, genres, decades, and more. There are classes on the platform in the following languages: German, Spanish, and English. There is a workout set to a musical playlist for every type of athlete on the Peloton platform. They have four types of intensity levels for classes: beginner, intermediate, advanced, and all levels. As a rule of thumb, all instructors teach classes across all levels. The classes vary in length from 5 minutes to 60+ minutes long. The most popular class lengths are 10, 20, and 30 minute long classes. Many instructors on the Peloton platform have a large following on social media. Devout fans often delineate their fandom by displaying the instructor's fan hashtag within the Peloton app. An athlete looking to take a class when feeling unmotivated should take a class with the instructor Robin Arzon, she's a no none-sense instructor who will motivate you from your core, you'll often find latino beats and hip hop music as the the themes in her playlists, which translate to a high energy environment pulling even the most unmotivated person into a workout. An athlete looking to take a class when sad should take a class with Christine D'Ercole. Her reflection ride classes might bring out a cry if you're feeling sad, but she leaves space for you to feel all your feelings and work through them with soothing tunes and motion. An athlete looking to take a class when they are angry should take a class with Kendal Toole. Kendal's class will help you channel that anger into an intense workout where you will be able to get all of the anger into the movements. Plus, she has an emotions themed class on anger. For an athlete looking to take a class when happy they should take a class with Callie Gullickson, her happy go lucky personality and goofy jokes will keep the good mood going. She's known for pop playlists with upbeat tunes. She loves Trader Joes and often makes references to it in her workout classes.

item.instruction: Write me a script for an upcoming All Hands meeting about our IPO prospects and how employees need to act in the quiet period.
item.reference: Lately, I've received plenty of questions about a potential IPO. I want to answer those questions today — and talk about how we as a company will answer questions like that moving forward. For years, we’ve shared that one of our aspirations is to build a wildly successful public company. Everyone has a role to play in getting us there and delivering for customers and growing the business is the most important thing most of us can do. A typical milestone on a high-growth journey is an IPO. But as companies get more serious about a potential IPO, there is a period where they stop talking about an IPO. This might be counter-intuitive, but here’s why: there are important regulatory restrictions on what companies can and cannot say when it comes to company growth and plans as they approach becoming a public company. The consequences if you don’t follow those rules can be serious — the SEC can even delay our ability to go public if it determines we’ve improperly promoted an IPO. And that’s obviously a situation we want to avoid, should we be in a position to go public in the future. And even language like this — "should we be in a position to go public in the future" — is vague. That's for a reason: as we get closer to an IPO, what we can say is restricted and we need to make sure we don’t make promises, otherwise regulators could force us to delay our plans. So I’m going to share some updates about how we’ll need to communicate related to a potential IPO: In order to preserve the ability to IPO at some point in the future, the executive team and I will not be sharing explicit details on our IPO journey or timing at All Hands or in other company communications. We also won’t be sharing updates to our market valuation. Hiring managers and recruiters should not explicitly talk about an IPO or our revenue growth with candidates. Instead, emphasize our massive opportunity, how we’re innovating, delivering value to our customers, and what an awesome team we have. We can’t engage with public market investors or financial journalists on certain topics. That means if a financial analyst, research analyst or reporter reaches out to you, don’t respond and forward the email to the communications team. We also can’t talk about a potential IPO on social media or with friends and family. You get the idea. I know that this will be different for us. We’ve always been a transparent company and this change is hopefully a short-term one. But it is an important one and you all have a role to play in helping us remain compliant. We all have different, important roles to play in making this company a successful, long-term business. The most important thing we can all do is to continue delivering for our customers and building a successful business.

item.instruction: Come up with a fictional account about a female housecat who stepped into a time machine and found herself in a 1970s shopping mall, armed only with a charge card. Include a bulleted list of 5 stores she visited and add an item she bought at each store, using the format of {department store} - {item}.
item.reference: Tabitha was a 5-year-old black housecat who was left alone all day by her family. She quickly grew bored with scratching up all of the furniture and taking naps on top of the bookcase, so she stood in the hallway, flicked at her whiskers, and said, "What can I do that I've never done before?" Tabitha then noticed that the laundry chute had been left open. With one leap, she jumped into it and slid down into the hamper in the basement. A big black box with an open door stood in the middle of the basement, equipped with flashing lights and a lit-up floor with a series of numbers. She knew that the box had been created by the scientist husband of the family, so she confidently jumped from the hamper and landed on the box's floor. Her four paws landed one after the other on the following numbers: "1," "9," "7," and "8." A sudden flash of light occurred, and Tabitha found herself in some strange building with two floors and a bunch of stores. A credit card appeared on the floor in front of her that had the word "master" on it. She figured that it was from her master, so it should be okay to use it. Putting it between her teeth, she jokingly said, "Fangs a lot, master!" She then sprinted forward and yelled, "Charge!" Here are five stores she visited, along with an item she "purchased" at each store: ( ● ) Filene's - A bottle of "Cat Got Your Tongue" perfume ( ● ) Camelot Music - a copy of Al Stewart's "Year Of The Cat" LP ( ● ) B. Dalton Bookseller - a copy of the book "Christmas Ideas For Cats" from Santa Paws ( ● ) F.W. Woolworth - a large plate of tuna casserole from the lunch counter ( ● ) Sear's - a family cat condo with a separate bathroom for Tabitha It quickly got "discovered" that the card account was fake. Before the local pound could snag her up in their net, another flash of light suddenly occurred. Tabitha found herself back at her house, standing in front of her master, who said "Chute! I left the laundry access open!" Unfortunately, Tabitha's purchases were not "past" over to the present, but at least she didn't have a boring day!

Jess arrived at the boy's house, her laughter echoing through the hallway as she stepped inside. The air smelled like garlic and rosemary, the scent of a home-cooked meal. Dinner was already on the table, a spread of roasted vegetables, grilled chicken, and a warm loaf of bread. The boy had made it all himself, and he was proud of it. He had been waiting for this moment, hoping it would be the start of something more.

As they sat down, he couldn't help but feel nervous. Jess was everything he had ever wanted—kind, smart, and beautiful. He wanted to impress her, to show her that he was more than just a boy with a weird hobby. He had been collecting things for years, but he never really told anyone about it. It was something he kept to himself, a secret that he had never shared with anyone.

He cleared his throat and said, “I have something to show you.” Jess looked up from her plate, curious. “What is it?” she asked, her eyes sparkling with interest.

He stood up and walked to the back of the room, where a small wooden box sat on the shelf. He opened it and pulled out a few items. “This is my collection,” he said, his voice a little shaky. “I’ve been collecting these for a long time.”

Jess leaned in, peering at the items in the box. “What are they?” she asked.

“They’re seeds,” he said, a little embarrassed. “I thought they were bones at first, but I was wrong. They’re just seeds.”

Jess laughed, a warm, genuine sound that made his heart skip a beat. “That’s not what I expected,” she said, her eyes still on the box. “But I guess it’s kind of cool, in a weird way.”

He smiled, relieved that she wasn’t upset. “I guess it is,” he said. “I just thought they looked like bones. I never really thought about what they actually were.”

Jess reached out and picked up one of the seeds, turning it in her hands. “They’re really small,” she said. “I can see why you thought they were bones.”

He nodded, feeling a little more at ease. “Yeah, they are. I guess I just like the way they look. They’re kind of like little treasures.”

Jess smiled at him, and for a moment, the world around them faded away. It was just the two of them, sharing a meal and a secret. The collection was just a part of him, and he hoped that Jess would see the person behind it.

item.reference: The boy awaits the girl. He fidgets. He's planned everything just right. He wants the afternoon to be perfect. He combed his hair and chose his favorite T-shirt, the striped one. He recalls his mother saying it brings out his eyes. Whatever that means. But Mum's a girl, so he reckons she knows something about what girls like. He has been thinking for a week about what girls like. The girl shows up with a small blue bow on the left side of her hair. The boy thinks she's splendid, though he'd never say so. They play jacks; they play cards. Mum makes them lemonade, then says, "Jess has to stay for dinner; her parents are running late. You two go play in the garden for a while. It's shady, and the boy is glad. She's staying for dinner. He hopes Mum will ask him to set the table. He'll place her sitting next to his. The boy and the girl sit on the rusty garden swing. Time passes. He glances over at her to see how she feels, but he can't tell. She is smiling, so that is something. "You want to see my collection? It's secret," he says. In his room, he pulls the shoebox from under the bed. When he stands, he senses how the girl steps closer. His skin prickles. He places the shoebox on the floor and sits cross-legged in front of it. He looks up at the girl and sees a series of conspiratorial afternoons like this together. His heart pounds when she sits opposite him, the musty box between them. He unwraps the contents, pulling old newspaper and tissue off as carefully as he can. In the bottom sit four small skulls. Dreadful eyes, large and oblong, drooping down. Noses flat and misshapen. Wide moaning mouths. The girl gasps and leans in for a closer inspection. "Careful," he says. "They're haunted." He showed this to his younger sister once, and she ran away screaming. The girl reaches out a light finger to touch the top of one of the skulls. "Can I hold it?" "Maybe next time." At dinner, their secrets fill the space between them. He worries over his small deception. He wonders when he'll tell her that his skulls are only ripe seed pods.

rounds.text: You discover time travel and travel to the summer of 2500. You find yourself in the middle of a music festival. The air is thick with sound, a symphony of futuristic beats and ancient melodies blending seamlessly. People in shimmering attire move in sync with the rhythm, their bodies glowing with the energy of the event. The festival grounds are vast, stretching beyond the horizon, with floating stages and holographic performers. You watch as a group of musicians, their faces hidden behind masks, create music that seems to manipulate the very air around them. The music is not just heard but felt, a force that connects every soul in the crowd. You step forward, drawn by the hypnotic pull of the sound, and feel the vibrations in your chest. The festival is more than a celebration of music; it is a living, breathing entity, a testament to the evolution of art and technology. You notice a stage where a single performer, dressed in a flowing suit of light, plays an instrument that looks like a fusion of a violin and a computer. The music they create is both familiar and alien, a bridge between past and future. You realize that this festival is a gathering of people from all eras, brought together by the universal language of music. The atmosphere is electric, filled with laughter, dancing, and the occasional burst of light from a performer's special effect. You feel a sense of belonging, as if you have always been part of this moment. The music guides you through the festival, leading you to different areas where each section has its own unique sound and style. You pass through a zone where the music is purely instrumental, a delicate balance of strings and synths, and then move into a section where voices blend with digital echoes, creating a hauntingly beautiful harmony. You stop at a small stage where a group of children, no older than ten, play a mix of traditional instruments and futuristic gadgets, their music full of innocence and creativity. You smile, realizing that music, in all its forms, is a constant in human history. As the festival continues, you feel the music enveloping you, a reminder of the power it holds to unite and inspire. You take a deep breath, the sound of the festival filling your lungs, and know that you are part of something greater than yourself. The music is eternal, and so is the festival.

item.reference: I awoke from my teleportation coma to the familiar refrain that haunts every music festival: " Shoulda seen Woodstock, man. I ’ m telling you, that shit was crazy." I raised my head on and saw the goodtime preacher and his congregation: all unwashed and unshaven, blind drunk, possibly high and obnoxiously loud. The leader's second in command lowered his ray bans and pointed at me like the first monkey to discover shit-flinging. " Holy hell bro, did you guys just see that? Dude just appeared outta thin air. Do that again man, my bros didn't see the first time." The blazing sun stung my eyes. I began to sway, my head aching, my throat as dry as the Colorado Desert. Colorado Desert? I could feel the unmistakable heat, the smell of crap and the din of a full sized hippie commune. I put the pieces together. " Don't tell me I ’ m at fucking Coachella" I howled. The nausea from travelling was too much: I fell over and began vomiting profusely on my teleportation suit. " Dude, what are you on?" queried the preacher. " Cause you couldn't like, help a brother out, could you?" He smirked as he asked this, but he extended a hand to help me up. Examining him and his friends, they all looked like normal college frat guys. I finally felt relieved. If I was in Coachella, then I had successfully discovered teleportation. But Coachella wasn't happening when I teleported… I groaned. " God, what year is it?" My bro friend was incredulous. " Dude, are you serious. Man, you are tripping like fuck right now. It ’ s Coachella, 2500." He was having me on. He must have been. " But your clothes?" I asked. " Yeah, it ’ s the new hipster line from Hollister" he told me a grin on his face. I could feel the bass thumping in the background. " But that's Nicki Minaj" I told him. " Well obviously we ’ re going to start the day with some classical music" the second in command informed me. " Of course" I responded meekly. I sat on the ground and gazed at the cerulean sky. It was the same peaceful and content sky I had always known. I was reassured that at least I had that. But the sky flickered, and for a second everything was grey with smog. " Shit, I hate it when the projector does that" sulked the second in command. The leader regarded me curiously. " Where are you from, man?" he asked me. " About 500 years in the past" I responded. This garnered some mild nods of approval amongst his disciples. " Ever go to Woodstock?" he asked.

Jesus, a man from the future, read a book that told the story of a man who became a leader through miracles. He decided to model his life after the main character, using his modern technology to travel back in time. With the help of his gadgets, he arrived in an ancient world where people worshipped gods and leaders. He believed that if he could perform miracles, he would be seen as a divine figure.

Jesus used his knowledge of science to create illusions that appeared as miracles. He made water turn into wine using a chemical formula, and he healed the sick with a device that emitted a special frequency. People were amazed and began to follow him, thinking he was a prophet. He spoke with wisdom, using data from his future to predict events and guide the people.

As his following grew, Jesus realized that the book he had read had a different ending. It warned that true leadership was not about performing miracles, but about serving others and teaching them to love one another. He had not read the end, and now he was caught in a cycle of power and influence that was not what he had intended.

Jesus tried to change his approach, but the people had already accepted him as their leader. He struggled with the weight of his actions, knowing that he had not truly followed the path of the book. He began to question whether his miracles had led to true faith or just temporary awe.

One day, a group of followers asked him to perform a miracle to prove his divinity. Jesus hesitated, remembering the book's warning. He decided to use his technology to create a simple act of kindness instead. He shared his food with the hungry and offered his knowledge to those in need. The people were touched, but they still saw him as a leader, not a teacher.

Jesus realized that his future had given him tools that could be used for good, but he had not fully understood the purpose of the book. He continued to walk with his followers, trying to guide them toward a deeper understanding of love and service. He used his technology not to impress, but to help, and slowly, the people began to see him not as a miracle worker, but as a man who had chosen to lead with compassion.

Despite his efforts, Jesus knew that the path he had taken was not the one the book had described. He had not read the end, and he was still learning. But with each act of kindness, he hoped to show the people that true leadership was not about miracles, but about the heart.

item.reference: So there ’ s this guy. He astounds audiences with his miracles. They clap, they cheer. They see him as more than man, more than mortal. But he dies, just like all of us. He dies and they cry, and they sit in disbelief. How could this happen, they yell. I feel so betrayed, so lost and left astray. And yet, within his death his legacy creates a lineage. A lineage that may not have existed without him. Of course it ’ s possible someone would have taken his place, become the person he was. I mean really it could have been anyone. The time was ripe for that kind of showmanship. The world needed him. So what is it, thousands of years later now, and Jesus Montero Smith spends his weekends in the vaults of the museums. Looking through the old manuscripts and documents of an age long forgotten, this man, this oracle of his time, revels in his new found immortality. That ’ s the beauty of the written word. All you need is an observant pair of eyes, and you live again. But Jesus is immediately taken by this story, by the simplicity of his ability to captivate, to bring out the best of others, to be more than a mere diversion. He is the innate representation of awe. So Jesus decides to check it out for himself. Setting the dial for 1904, and unbinding the handcuffs of time, travels back to see him. Jesus wasn ’ t so interested in the miracles so much as how he could illicit such a response. Jesus wanted to experience the unknown. He lives in a time where everything has an answer. The past, the present, even the future; they exist on an even plane, and infinite understanding of temporal reality. Jesus finds himself in a crowd, and he waits. And finally it happens, and the crowd goes wild, and the miraculous nature of everything is like a tidal wave. Of course it doesn ’ t matter how any of the miracles are actually accomplished. That ’ s not the point. There ’ s a comfort in believing in something beyond yourself. In something that provides a glimmer of hope that there ’ s more than meets the eye. Of course Jesus knows what happens when you die. Of course Jesus knows it ’ s all showmanship. Jesus knows that the man will die in a few years still relatively young. But for a moment he was able to revel in the magic of uncertainty, even as a false creation, even as an expected notion.

item.instruction: Discuss the pros and cons of a day trip to Vancouver versus a day trip to Portland from Seattle.
item.reference: Both Vancouver, Canada and Portland, Oregon can be a fun day trip from Seattle. The pros for both are that the cities are fairly close to Seattle, so a day trip is very reasonable. In terms of time to get there, Portland is a bit closer and also has the advantage of still being in the United States. So, you may save time compared to going to Vancouver since there is no border crossing. This difference can be fairly trivial though since the border between the US and Canada is often fairly fast. Besides travel time, something to consider is what kind of activity you want to do. Vancouver has a lot of great chinese cuisine and also has Stanley park which is a great place to go walking and cycling. Portland is known for Voodoo donuts, a popular and unique donut store. Overall, both are great options and it boils down to what things you enjoy doing most.

item.instruction: Running a business is tough and there will always be problems in the market. Make the case to a skeptical colleague as to why private sector managers should devote attention and energy to being a steward of the institutions of capitalism. Please include citations for Jonathan Haidt.
item.reference: To steward means to take care of, to guide, and it implies a sense of responsibility. I agree with the notion that, in addition to stories about capitalism prevailing as either an extractor or savior, a third story can be written of “prosperity with problems” in which participants are grateful for accomplishments yet pursuing improvements (Haidt, J.) Putting that together, then, who is responsible for writing this story? I believe that answer to be business leaders themselves -- or else be beholden to government regulation to steward the institution in the direction that benefits not just owners and shareholders, but all stakeholders including employees and the environment. But why should business leaders steward the market? Private managers hold a moral obligation to those relying on capitalism for work and health insurance to create sustainable jobs. As individuals count on business leaders to respond to our world’s most prevalent issues, business leaders also hold a social obligation to do so with care. This response also assigns the appropriate accountability to whomever is responsible for perpetuating a system – if business leaders want to reap the rewards of profit, they must assume responsibility for the very conditions which benefit them. As alluded to above, private interests sometimes conflict horribly with what society and individuals need, so government regulators must be stewards alongside business leaders. Additionally, business leaders can take a step away from their day-to-day and learn from those who have dedicated their lives to research.

As a critic with a discerning palate for children’s literature, I found the book to be a curious blend of charm and didacticism. The narrative, told through the voice of the Once-ler, is both engaging and slightly didactic, which may not appeal to all young readers. The illustrations, while colorful and whimsical, lack the depth and intricacy one might expect from a more refined children’s book. The Lorax himself is a memorable character, with his distinctive voice and persistent nature, but his role feels somewhat secondary to the moral of the story. The book’s message, though well-intentioned, is delivered with a heavy hand, which may detract from its overall appeal. Despite these shortcomings, *The Lorax* remains a notable entry in the children’s canon, offering a gentle introduction to ecological awareness. It is not without its flaws, but it does succeed in sparking conversation. For a critic with a refined taste, it is a book that is more than it seems, yet less than it could be.

item.reference: Title: Review of “The Lorax”: Real or Imaginary? As a highly respected children’s literature critic, I know I had to dive into Dr. Seuss’ “The Lorax” with a mix of curiosity and skepticism. I, of course, have to be honest and say I definitely had my doubts about whether or not the book would still stand the test of time for today’s children. But as I read each and every page, I was able to find a certain kind of depth in this story that went far beyond funny pictures and words. If any of my readers are unfamiliar with the plotline, the Lorax is a mustachioed creature who is the environment’s protector. He speaks out against the Once-ler, who represents corporate greed. The truffula trees and bar-ba-loots are endangered, and the Lorax urges others to care. “The Lorax” is more than zany pictures and childish rhymes. It is really a metaphor regarding the environment on Earth. Dr. Seuss deserves some praise for being able to translate a confusing-yet-important topic for children. After all, they say children will inherit the Earth, right?

They taught him to be alert, to trust his instincts, and to find beauty in the chaos. Marco had always felt a connection to the city, as if the streets whispered secrets only he could hear. One night, after his parents had gone to sleep, he slipped out of the apartment and wandered into the darkened streets.

He met a group of teenagers who shared stories of resilience and hope, not fear. In a quiet park, he found a hidden garden where people gathered to talk, laugh, and heal. The city was alive with voices that didn’t make it into the headlines, and Marco began to see the Bronx not just as a place of danger, but as a place of strength and community.

They had taught him to look beyond the surface, to find light in the shadows. As he returned home, he felt a sense of belonging that no news report could ever capture. The Bronx was more than the headlines said—it was a place of hidden wonders, where every corner held a story waiting to be discovered. Marco had found his own, and it was beautiful.

The story should include the kid exploring the Bronx at night and finding out there is more to the city than what’s in the news. There should be 3 paragraphs and the beginning of each sentence for the paragraphs should spell NYC.
item.reference: Nighttime in the Bronx isn’t exactly safe. As the daytime exposure dwindles, the misfits of the evening arise. The AM news often reports on matters that happen after the sun sets. The rowdy crowds that break things in a drunken stupor. The robberies and murders take place in the alleys. Hearing such scary news, my parents always barked at me to stay home after dark. Yet being cooped up at home is never fun, especially when you live with your parents, who just happen to be 2 Dalmatians. Sure, it’s fun to throw the ball around with them, but I don’t want to do that the entire time. I’m 14, and I just want to get away from those 2. So, after they fall asleep, I’m going to leave the house and see what the night has to offer. Carefully, I slip out the back door once my parent's light turns off. When I get to the street corner, what I saw amazed me. I expected the streets to be blotted with dim city lights and shadowy figures, but instead, I saw fire walkers, unfazed by the hot rocks they stood upon. There were dancers covered in colorful fabrics waking up and down. Sure, I saw some shady stuff happen, but that doesn’t take away from the levity I saw. The street was filled with life. It was literally night and day, from my expectations. I can’t wait to see what else the city has to offer.

I was born in the field, a green cucumber, plump and full of life. The sun warmed my skin, and the earth gave me strength. I grew tall, reaching for the sky, my leaves stretching wide to catch the morning dew. I was part of a family, a row of cousins, all growing together, sharing the same soil and sun.

One day, a hand reached down and pulled me from the earth. I was taken to a place where the air was cooler, and the light was different. I was placed in a crate with my siblings, and we were taken to a kitchen where the smells were strong and the sounds were loud. A woman with a kind smile looked at me and said, “You’ll be a pickle.”

I was cut, salted, and placed in a jar. The brine was cold and sharp, and I felt a strange tingling as it touched my skin. I was submerged, surrounded by my new home. The jar was sealed, and I was placed on a shelf in the pantry, where the light was dim and the air was still.

Days passed, and I changed. My skin turned a deep green, and my taste became sharp and tangy. I was no longer the cucumber I once was. I had become something new, something preserved. I was no longer growing, but I was still alive in a different way.

The pantry was full of jars like me, each holding a story, a memory, a transformation. I was part of a collection, a group of pickles, each with its own history. I was stored away, waiting for the time when someone would open me and take a bite.

The seasons changed, and the world outside grew colder. The field where I was born was now bare, the leaves long gone, the soil frozen. I remained in the jar, untouched, waiting. I was not forgotten, but I was not used either. I was a part of the home, a quiet presence in the corner of the pantry.

One day, a hand reached for me. A child, wide-eyed and curious, opened the jar and took a bite. The flavor was strong, the taste sharp and bright. I was used, but I was also appreciated. I had become something more than I was before.

I was no longer a cucumber, but I was still part of the field, part of the earth, part of the cycle. I had been transformed, and in that transformation, I had found my purpose. I was a pickle, and I was ready to be enjoyed.

item.instruction: Write a story from the perspective of a pickle as it is going from a cucumber in the field to being jarred and put away for the year.
item.reference: I am a pickle. Well, no that isn't quite right, I'm a cucumber right now but soon I will be a pickle. Days ago some friendly hands picked me up from my nice sunny patch in the field. I was about ready to come in, to be honest, the heat was getting to me and there were far too many rabbits lurking around. It was very nice to be carried inside, given a nice cool bath, and set aside for the night to sleep and relax. I woke up a bit later than usual still surrounded in the colander by my other cucumber friends. They were still sleeping so I did my best not to disturb them. They weren't a talkative bunch normally anyway. The sun was just starting to peak in through the curtains above the sink when a lady entered the room. The same lady who grabbed me from the patch yesterday. She seemed very friendly and nice. At least I thought so until she picked me up, bowl and all, and gave me a big shake. What a way to rise and shine. I could hear the other cucumbers grumbling too. She transported us a few feet away to another part of the countertop. Then, the lady mixed a bunch of ingredients in a big pot on the stove and it started to smell good but it also tickled my nose a bit. Perhaps a bit too garlicky for my tastes. Next thing I knew she was picking me up again but this time she stuck me in a jar! I couldn't believe it, it was finally happening! It's the most exciting day in any gherkins life. A few of my other cucumber friends joined me and we all nestled up close to each other. It was very cozy and everyone had a nice view through the glass too. Then, the nice lady gave us a warm bath. It felt even nicer than the cool bath I had before. It had hints of dill and pepper and it covered me from my tippy toes all the way to the top of my head. She put a nice little roof over top sealing me in. And I knew that from this day forward I was a cucumber no more, now I was one proud pickle.

item.reference: It's great that you're taking proactive steps to alleviate the symptoms you typically experience after drinking. Here are some additional tips that may help: 1. Eat before and during your drinking session. Drinking on an empty stomach can lead to faster absorption of alcohol and more severe hangover symptoms the next day. Eating a balanced meal before and during drinking can help slow the absorption of alcohol and reduce the severity of hangover symptoms. 2. Choose your drinks wisely. Different types of alcohol can have varying levels of congeners, which are impurities that can worsen hangover symptoms. Generally, darker liquors like whiskey and red wine have higher levels of congeners. Clear liquors like vodka and gin tend to have lower levels. 3. Stay hydrated. Drinking water between alcoholic drinks is a good start, but it's also important to hydrate throughout the day and night. Drinking a glass of water before bed can also help prevent dehydration and alleviate hangover symptoms the next day. 4. Get enough sleep. Alcohol can disrupt your sleep, so getting a good night's rest can help your body recover and reduce the severity of hangover symptoms. 5. Consider taking an over-the-counter pain reliever like ibuprofen or aspirin to help alleviate headaches. It's worth noting that everyone's tolerance for alcohol and their hangover symptoms can vary, so it's important to pay attention to how your body reacts and adjust accordingly. It's also a good idea to have a plan for how to get home safely after drinking, whether that means having a designated driver or using a ride-sharing service.

item.reference: Two men well within their late forties, wearing pristine, white lab coats, walk into a bar near the dead of night. No one takes notice of the two. The crowd was the usual lot - too down and drunk to care about two oddly dressed fellows. One woman sitting at the back corner swigs down her shot of tequila while gradually slumping down into her seat. Up front, a man, sporting a baseball cap, was vehemently arguing with the nearby pole whether the Giants would win this season. The bartender was making small talk with his newer customers about the weather while he prepared their drinks in an overly flamboyant manner. The two men took their seats at the front of the bar and glanced at each other every so often as if to communicate through blinks. They were nervous. They've never done anything like this. The bartender finally comes around to their area and asks, " What will it be today, fine gentlemen." The man, sitting on the right, takes the lead and replies, " Have you heard the joke where two scientist walk into a bar?" With a disappointed wrinkle forming over his forehead, the bartender sighs " I'm not here to listen to your jokes, do you want anything to drink?" " Good because this isn't a joke; it's a robbery," says the man, sitting on the left, as he produces a vial out from the his lab coat. Instantly, the room smells of rotten eggs causing some patrons to gag. " This is sulfuric acid. It won't kill you; we aren't that cruel. But it will severely scar your face. Now give us all your money and a glass of H20" " Yes, I'll take a glass of H2O, too," agreed the other man. The two men finish their drinks, take the money, and make a clean get away because this isn't a joke. It's a robbery.

The employee of the month's day was a day of quiet dread. It was not a celebration, but a reckoning. The chosen one, the most proficient sinner, stood at the center of the office, a figure both revered and reviled. Their name was whispered with a mix of fear and admiration, for they had mastered the art of sinning with precision and flair. They had learned the rules of the game, twisted them to their advantage, and emerged victorious.

Each month, the office would gather for the ceremony, a ritual of sorts. The employee of the month was not just recognized for their work, but for their ability to push boundaries, to outdo their peers, to make the lesser ones feel the weight of their own inadequacies. It was a day of judgment, not of praise, for the true purpose was not to honor, but to torment.

The lesser employees, those who had not reached the pinnacle of sinfulness, were left to endure the consequences of their own mediocrity. They were the ones who had failed to rise, to outshine, to outmaneuver. They were the ones who had not mastered the art of deception, the art of bending rules, the art of making others feel small. And on this day, they were made to feel it all the more.

The employee of the month would stand before the group, a figure of authority, a judge of their own making. They would speak, not with words of encouragement, but with a tone that carried the weight of judgment. They would recount the sins of the lesser ones, not in anger, but in a way that made it clear that they had been outdone. They would speak of missed deadlines, of poor performance, of lack of ambition, as if these were not just mistakes, but failures.

The lesser employees would sit in silence, their faces a mixture of shame and resentment. They would look at the employee of the month, not with admiration, but with a deep-seated envy. They would wish they had been more cunning, more ruthless, more willing to cross the line. They would wish they had been the one to rise, to be recognized, to be the judge.

And yet, the employee of the month would not be punished. They would be celebrated, not for their work, but for their ability to sin with skill. They would be given a trophy, a certificate, a moment of glory. They would be the one to decide the fate of the lesser ones, to determine what torments they would endure. It was a cruel irony, for the one who had sinned the most was the one who had the power to decide the punishment of others.

They would carry the memory of the employee of the month's day with them, a reminder of what they had failed to achieve. item.reference: Satan seemed excised to announce the employee of the month. Of course, Mr. Hitler had been amazing, but Stalin has been just as good at tormenting as the former. He had once made a dog killer's punishment to be eaten alive by dogs and then regenerate, thus causing the cycle to repeat for infinity. Another punishment was for one of Hitler's guards who had been in hiding, but he had not really done that much other then order a single gassing, which made Hitler want him to suffer for being so slothful. So, Stalin suggested that he would be pumped full of food while watching footage of gassings. Of course Hitler loved the idea, and it was put into action. Of course, if he thought of all of the eternal punishments, he would miss the meeting. He opened the door, only to see the worst men and woman to ever grace the earth, which was fine for Satan. He walked up to the podium. " Hello employees. As you may know, I am here to announce who gets the title of employee of the month. You all know him as the guy who managed to brain wash a bunch of people and rule Russia with a iron fist, Mr. Stalin!" Stalin walked up to the podium. Satan handed over the award to the mustached man. " Thank you ever so much Satan! I would like to give a shout out to my best friend Hitler, who I have forgiven for trying to invade Mother Country Russia!" Hitler seemed excited. " Your the man!" he shouted. " I would also love the give a thank you to Vlad the Impaler, who deserved last month's award, and who is a great friend as well!" Vlad seemed pretty happy to be mentioned as well, as he shouted; " YOUR THE MAN!!" Stalin then continued. " Last but not least, Vlad's amazing fiance, who is a very good tormentor, Elizabeth the blood countess!" Of course she was sitting right next to Vlad, holding his hand because they were soulmates. They both LOVED killing their subjects, and they both enjoyed seeing those lesser then them suffer. " Thank you so much Stalin! Besides, Vlad is much more loving then my previous husband, who I was engaged to at ELEVEN!! I could go on with how we met, but i'd rather not." Stalin and the rest of his coworkers knew that we would be married on next Wednesday, and that everybody was invited. rounds.text: They said I was the most bitter in my circle, because I constantly mock and make fun of my lovelorn friends and their (beautiful) love lives. I don’t think that’s true. I think they just don’t understand me. I don’t mock them. I don’t make fun of their love lives. I just don’t care. I don’t think love is something that should be taken seriously. I think it’s a distraction, a waste of time, and a reason for people to act foolishly. I don’t want to be like them, caught up in some romantic fantasy that will eventually end in heartbreak. I’ve seen it happen too many times. I’ve watched my friends go through the same cycle over and over again, chasing after someone who doesn’t deserve them, only to be left behind when they finally realize it. I don’t want that. I don’t want to be in love. I don’t want to be hurt. I don’t want to be the one who’s left standing in the rain, crying because someone else chose someone else. I think that’s what makes me bitter. Not because I’m angry or resentful, but because I’ve seen it all before. I’ve seen the pain, the heartache, the disappointment. I’ve seen how love can turn people into something they’re not. I don’t want to be like that. I don’t want to be someone who’s in love. I think that’s what they don’t understand. They think I’m bitter because I don’t have a love life, but I don’t think that’s the case. I think I’m just different. I think I’ve made a choice to live my life without love, without the complications that come with it. I don’t think I’m bitter. I think I’m just realistic. item.reference: God damn Sarah is updating her Instagram again with dozens of pictures of the flowers Jack gave her to congratulate her graduating law school. Jack, the star pediatrician in the district who could heal children with just a smile. What Jack doesn't know because he was never her friend in high school was that Sarah puked into the punch bowl in prom. Not exactly a romantic image, huh, Jack? Then there's Mister I'm-Perfect-and-My-Life-Is-Perfect Christopher who just loves to rub it in people's faces that he's the happiest married man on the planet. Chris has a jaw and body that could only be matched by his husband Nathan. They got matching tattoos for reaching the summit of Kilimanjaro together and adopted 2.5 kids and half a dog. My only comfort is that Nathan has a crooked nose and limp. From serving in Afghanistan. And Rachel, oh Rachel. I thought she was going to be in the always solo train with me for the whole ride, but no, she got off a stop called " Norwegian Reggae Club". I know the world has nearly seven billion people, but there could only be a handful who even know of the genre, let alone be enthusiastic enough to start a club in some artsy-fartsy cafe that serves cruelty free coffee and gives away free meals for the homeless in which Rachel could find love. I'm not bitter. No really, I'm not. I'm not! A lot of people think that I scowl and mock my positively diabetes-inducing friends because I've never felt love and wouldn't understand it. They don't know my story, and I don't mean that in the edgy Marilyn Manson-quoting, self-help-book-consuming way. I knew someone. They laughed at everything like every exhalation would be their last; they laughed so deeply in such a way that it caught my soul and made it lighter. They held me as if I were an idol, every touch leaving prayer and longing on my starved skin. They smiled at me and all I would think of is how the sun left glitter on water as it set, the reflection calling cards that said, " Look at me, notice me before I go away!" Afternoon naps. Whispered poems. Stargazing, hushed dreams shared between each other as if just articulating them would make them come true. Indulgent midnight cakes. Dancing, spinning so that the world was just a blur, just them and I. The future. The past. " Promise me..." I-love-you's said and unsaid. I know my friends, and I know what love is like. But one day, the roses will wilt and the music will stop, and they'll wonder if they'll ever live like that ever again, without the disgust, fear, and mistakes of everyday life. They'll wonder, and nobody will be there to answer them.
